questions.problem:
Which of the following equations is a Bernoulli differential equation?

- ${y}^{′}-\sqrt{x}\,y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{y}$
- ${y}^{′}+y\operatorname{tan}⁡x=-\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}$ $$
- ${y}^{′}-{y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x={y}^{6}$
questions.worked_solution:
A Bernoulli differential equation has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n},
$$

where $n$ is a real number.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Equation I is a Bernoulli differential equation. In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\sqrt{x},\,q(x)={x}^{3},\,n=-1.
$$

- Equation II is a Bernoulli differential equation. In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,q(x)=-\sqrt{x},\,n=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

- Equation III is *not* a Bernoulli differential equation. It is missing the $p(x)y$ term.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.

questions.problem:
Which of the following equations is a Bernoulli differential equation?

- ${y}^{′}-{e}^{x}{y}^{2}=\sqrt{y}$
- ${y}^{3}{y}^{′}+{y}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡x=\sqrt{y}$
- $y\,{y}^{′}+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y={cos}^{2}⁡y$
questions.worked_solution:
A Bernoulli differential equation has the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n},
$$

where $n$ is a real number.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Equation I is *not* a Bernoulli differential equation. It is missing the $p(x)y$ term.

- Equation II is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
{y}^{′}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)y={y}^{-5/2}
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,\,q(x)=1,\,n=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

- Equation III is *not* a Bernoulli differential equation.  If we attempt to write the equation in standard form, we get

$$
{y}^{′}+x(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{y})=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡y}{y}.
$$

It is missing both the $p(x)y$ and $q(x){y}^{n}$ terms.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+3xy=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=3x,\,q(x)=-{x}^{4},\,n=3.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}+3x{y}^{-2}=-{x}^{4}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3xz=-{x}^{4}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-6xz=2{x}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-6x.$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-y\operatorname{tan}⁡x={y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,n=5.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{5},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-5}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-4{y}^{-5}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-5}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{4}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+4z\operatorname{tan}⁡x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x\sqrt{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{{y}^{1/2}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\,z=x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{2x}\,z=\frac{x}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=\frac{x}{2}.$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-y(2x+3{y}^{2})=0
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-y(2x+3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy-3{y}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy & =3{y}^{3} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}y & =3{x}^{-2}{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-2{x}^{-1},\,q(x)=3{x}^{-2},\,n=3.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}{y}^{-2}=3{x}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2{x}^{-1}z=3{x}^{-2}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+4{x}^{-1}z=-6{x}^{-2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-6{x}^{-2}.$

$$

$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{2},\,q(x)=x,\,n=4.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{-3}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{y}^{-4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

$$
-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z=x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2}z=-3x.

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}-xy.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{-1/2}-xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy & ={y}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{-1}y & ={x}^{-2}{y}^{-1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{-1},\,q(x)={x}^{-2},\,n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we multiply the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{-1}{y}^{3/2}={x}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{-1}z={x}^{-2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1}z=\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-2}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{3}{2x},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{2{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/2x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(3/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{3/2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3/2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1}z) & ={x}^{3/2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-2}) \\ {x}^{3/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2}z & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2}z) & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3/2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{2}{x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{3/2}z & =3{x}^{1/2}+C \\ z & =\frac{3\sqrt{x}+C}{{x}^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3/2}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{3/2}=\frac{3\sqrt{x}+C}{{x}^{3/2}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{{(3\sqrt{x}+C)}^{2/3}}{x}\,.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{{y}^{-1}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x}\,⇒\,y=\frac{3x}{C-{x}^{3}}\,.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}+2xy}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}+2xy}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2{x}^{-1}y & ={x}^{-2}{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-2{x}^{-1},\,q(x)={x}^{-2},\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}{y}^{-1}={x}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2{x}^{-1}z={x}^{-2}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2{x}^{-1}z=-{x}^{-2}
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2{x}^{-1}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (-{x}^{-2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =-\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & =-x+C \\ z & =\frac{C-x}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-x}{{x}^{2}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{C-x}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+xz=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-xz=-x
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-x,\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-xz) & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}\cdot (-x) \\ {e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-xz{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2} & =-x{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}) & =-x{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2})\,\text{d}x & =-\int x{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{-{x}^{2}/2} & ={e}^{-{x}^{2}/2}+C \\ z & =1+C{e}^{{x}^{2}/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=1+C{e}^{{x}^{2}/2}\,⇒\,y=\frac{1}{1+C{e}^{{x}^{2}/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-{e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{x} & =-{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{C-{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following equations is a Bernoulli differential equation?

- $y\,y' + x^2y^2 = e^x y^4$

- $xy' + x^3y = -x^2 y^3$

- $y' + y\cos{x} = e^{y+1}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A Bernoulli differential equation has the form

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n,
$$

where $n$ is a real number.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Equation I is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = e^x y^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) = e^x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation II is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = -xy^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) =-x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation III is *not* a Bernoulli differential equation. It is missing the $q(x)y^n$ term.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Reducing a Bernoulli Differential Equation to First Order Linear
canonical_examples.problem:
The substitution $z=y^m$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}}
$$

into an equation of the form $z'(x) + P(x)z(x) = Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = x^3, \qquad q(x) = 1, \qquad n=-\dfrac12.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
y^{1/2} \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y^{3/2}= 1.\qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = \dfrac{3}{2}y^{1/2} \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^{1/2}\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(\ast)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + x^3\,z = 1
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{3}{2}x^3z = \dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad q(x) = x^2, \qquad n=-1.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by $y^{-1},$ and we get

$$
y \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{x}= x^2.
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{1}{x}z  = x^2
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{2}{x} z
		=2x^2
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2{x}^{2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =2{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2}) & =2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{2} & =\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{2{x}^{5}+C}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5C_1.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z=y^{2}.$ This results in the general solution

$$
y^{ 2} =\dfrac{2x^5 + C}{5x^2}.
$$
